claim: DHFR is encoded by the folA gene and is essential for the biosynthesis of purines, dTTP, glycine and methionine.
source: DHFR is encoded by the folA gene and is essential for the biosynthesis of purines, dTTP, glycine and methionine.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DHFR function in E. coli.

claim: D27 mutations in DHFR were introduced in E. coli chromosome by lambda red recombination.
source: Mutations in key D27 catalytic residue of DHFR were introduced in E. coli chromosome, together with flanking antibiotic resistant markers, by lambda red recombination and strains devoid of DHFR function were selected with antibiotics in folAmix-containing agar plates.
evidence: The figure caption describes the experimental procedure used to create the mutant strains.

claim: D27 mutants are lethal but fitness can be partially rescued by metabolic compensation with folAmix.
source: D27 mutants are lethal but fitness can be partially rescued by metabolic compensation with folAmix.
evidence: Figure 1B shows this relationship and the text describes the experimental observation.

claim: The carboxylate side chain in position 27 is strictly conserved among 290 bacterial DHFR orthologues, where Asp and Glu are present at a frequency of 82% and 18%, respectively.
source: The presence of a carboxylate side chain in position 27 is strictly conserved among 290 bacterial DHFR orthologues, where Asp and Glu are present at a frequency of 82% and 18%, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: D27 mutant proteins have catalytic efficiencies (kcat/KM) several orders of magnitude lower than wild type.
source: The catalytic activity measurements confirm the lack of significant DHFR function in these variants; catalytic efficiencies (kcat/KM) are several orders of magnitude lower than wild type.
evidence: This is supported by the kinetic measurements presented in Table 1.

claim: D27F mutant has a catalytic efficiency that is 2 × 10^-7 relative to wild type.
source: Table 1
evidence: The table shows measured kcat/KM values for D27F mutant relative to wild type.

claim: D27N mutant has a catalytic efficiency that is 4 × 10^-5 relative to wild type.
source: Table 1
evidence: The table shows measured kcat/KM values for D27N mutant relative to wild type.

claim: D27G mutant has a catalytic efficiency that is 3 × 10^-5 relative to wild type.
source: Table 1
evidence: The table shows measured kcat/KM values for D27G mutant relative to wild type.

claim: The thermal stability of D27 mutant proteins is mostly unaffected or even significantly increased in the case of D27F mutant.
source: However, thermal denaturation data obtained for the D27 mutant proteins indicates that their stability is mostly unaffected (or even significantly increased in the case of D27F mutant; Tian et al., 2015) showing that, despite the lack of catalytic activity, these proteins retain the ability to fully fold.
evidence: This is based on thermal denaturation measurements and supported by a citation.

claim: D27F mutant has a ΔTm of +7.6 ± 0.1 °C compared to wild type.
source: Table 1
evidence: The table shows measured thermal stability data for D27F mutant.

claim: No DHFR activity could be detected in cell lysates of D27 mutant strains.
source: When DHFR function was assayed in cell lysates of D27 mutant strains, no DHFR activity could be detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C), confirming that these mutations inactivate DHFR function in the cell.
evidence: This is based on enzymatic activity measurements in cell lysates shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: D27 mutants grow only at high concentrations of folAmix.
source: As expected, growth experiments showed that D27 mutants grow only at high concentrations of folAmix (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth rate measurements at various folAmix concentrations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The growth rates measured for all D27 mutants at high folAmix fall in the range 70–80% of wild type.
source: The growth rates measured for all D27 mutants at high folAmix fall in the range 70–80% of wild type and lag times were typically 1.5–2 fold longer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on growth rate measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lag times for D27 mutants were typically 1.5–2 fold longer than wild type.
source: The growth rates measured for all D27 mutants at high folAmix fall in the range 70–80% of wild type and lag times were typically 1.5–2 fold longer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on growth measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Proteins involved in central processes were significantly downregulated in D27F strain, including energy metabolism (aerobic respiration, TCA cycle), metabolism of nitrogen, several amino acids, pyrimidines and lipopolysaccharides.
source: Proteins involved in central processes were significantly downregulated in D27F strain, including energy metabolism (aerobic respiration, TCA cycle), metabolism of nitrogen, several amino acids, pyrimidines and lipopolysaccharides.
evidence: This is based on proteomics analysis comparing D27F mutant to wild type.

claim: There was significant increase in the expression of proteins involved in stress responses, peptidoglycan recycling and salvage of guanine and xanthine in D27F strain.
source: On the other end, we found significant increase in the expression of proteins involved in stress responses, peptidoglycan recycling and salvage of guanine and xanthine.
evidence: This is based on proteomics analysis comparing D27F mutant to wild type.

claim: The metabolism of purines, pyrimidines, beta-alanine, histidine and sulfur were the most significantly changed in D27F mutant comparatively to wild type.
source: The analysis revealed that the metabolism of purines, pyrimidines, beta-alanine, histidine and sulfur were the most significantly changed in D27F mutant comparatively to wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: This is based on metabolomics enrichment analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Metabolites upstream the reactions that require reduced folate cofactors (PurT, PurH, and ThyA) build up in D27F mutant.
source: Not surprisingly, we observe build-up of metabolites upstream the reactions that require reduced folate cofactors (PurT, PurH, and ThyA), whereas metabolites downstream of those reactions are found to be strongly depleted.
evidence: This is based on metabolomics analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Metabolites downstream of reactions requiring reduced folate cofactors are strongly depleted in D27F mutant.
source: Not surprisingly, we observe build-up of metabolites upstream the reactions that require reduced folate cofactors (PurT, PurH, and ThyA), whereas metabolites downstream of those reactions are found to be strongly depleted.
evidence: This is based on metabolomics analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Three trajectories (1,3 and 6) of D27G evolution reached the ability to grow in the complete absence of folAmix.
source: Three trajectories (1,3 and 6) stand out by reaching the ability to grow in the complete absence of folAmix.
evidence: This is based on the evolutionary experiment data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In all three trajectories (1,3 and 6) of D27G evolution that reverted phenotype, residue Gly27 had mutated to cysteine.
source: Accordingly, Sanger sequencing analysis of this region revealed that in all these three trajectories (1,3 and 6), but not trajectory 4, residue Gly27 had mutated to cysteine.
evidence: This is based on Sanger sequencing data of evolved strains.

claim: Cysteine does not occur naturally in position 27 among known DHFR sequences; only aspartate or glutamate are observed in this locus.
source: This finding was surprising because alignment of multiple known DHFR sequences shows that cysteine does not occur naturally in position 27; only aspartate or glutamate are observed in this locus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: D27C mutant has a catalytic efficiency that is 2 × 10^-3 relative to wild type.
source: Table 1
evidence: The table shows measured kcat/KM values for D27C mutant relative to wild type.

claim: A biophysical model predicts a growth rate of about 30% of the wild type strain for D27C mutant.
source: Taking as input the in vitro biophysical properties of purified D27C mutant, namely kcat/KM and bis-ANS fluorescence values, the model predicts a growth rate of about 30% of the wild type strain.
evidence: This is based on a previously established fitness prediction model (Rodrigues et al., 2016) applied to D27C mutant data.

claim: The measured growth rate of reconstituted D27C strain was 92% of the wild type.
source: This strain was able to grow in the absence of folAmix supplementation, and the measured growth rate was 92% of the wild type, which is in fair agreement with the in vitro-based prediction which does not take into account a possibility of upregulation in response to DHFR deficiency (Bershtein et al., 2015a) (see Material and methods section Predicting fitness of D27 mutants for discussion) (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is based on growth rate measurements of the reconstituted D27C strain shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: D27C mutation is associated with a dramatic 4 orders of magnitude increase in the inhibition constant for trimethoprim.
source: Of note is also the fact that the significant loss in catalytic efficiency in D27C mutant is associated with a dramatic 4 orders of magnitude increase in the inhibition constant for trimethoprim, and consequent nearly 100-fold increased resistance of the D27C strain to trimethoprim inhibition in comparison with the wild type (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on inhibition constant measurements shown in Table 1 and resistance measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: D27C strain shows nearly 100-fold increased resistance to trimethoprim inhibition compared to wild type.
source: Of note is also the fact that the significant loss in catalytic efficiency in D27C mutant is associated with a dramatic 4 orders of magnitude increase in the inhibition constant for trimethoprim, and consequent nearly 100-fold increased resistance of the D27C strain to trimethoprim inhibition in comparison with the wild type (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on dose-response measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: IC50 for trimethoprim was determined to be 0.8 ± 0.1 µg/mL for wild type and 79 ± 17 µg/mL for D27C mutant.
source: The data was fitted with a logistic equation (solid lines) from which IC50 was determined to be 0.8 ± 0.1 µg/mL for wild type and 79 ± 17 µg/mL for D27C mutant.
evidence: This is based on dose-response curve fitting shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Active site mutations compromise catalytic function but also disrupt pocket interactions with the drug, resulting in high levels of resistance.
source: This is in line with previous observations that active site mutations compromise catalytic function but also disrupt pocket interactions with the drug, resulting in high levels of resistance (Bader et al., 2006; Rodrigues et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Evolutionary trajectories of D27F and D27N mutants show a marked decrease in folAmix necessary to sustain growth, in most cases reaching concentrations nearly three orders of magnitude lower than initially required for naïve strains.
source: Evolutionary trajectories of D27F and D27N mutants represented in Figure 4A and B, respectively, show a marked decrease in folAmix necessary to sustain growth, in most cases reaching concentrations nearly three orders of magnitude lower than initially required for naïve strains.
evidence: This is based on the evolutionary experiment data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Individual colonies taken among all trajectories that adapted to low folAmix concentrations all showed a strikingly similar phenotype - folAmix-dependent growth profile, irrespective of the initial variant at D27 locus (F/N and also trajectory four in D27G).
source: We found that individual colonies taken among all trajectories that adapted to low folAmix concentrations all showed a strikingly similar phenotype - folAmix-dependent growth profile, irrespective of the initial variant at D27 locus (F/N and also trajectory four in D27G) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is based on growth measurements of individual clones shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Evolved D27N and D27F strains cannot grow in the complete absence of folAmix.
source: However, these strains cannot grow in the complete absence of folAmix.
evidence: This is based on growth measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No mutations were found in folA locus in evolved D27N and D27F strains.
source: Accordingly, no mutations were found in folA locus in evolved D27N and D27F strains (see Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The growth rate of the evolved strains measured at high concentrations of folAmix reached values comparable to wild type.
source: The growth rate of the evolved strains measured at high concentrations of folAmix reached values comparable to wild type, showing a clear fitness increase with respect to naïve strain.
evidence: This is based on growth rate measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At lower concentrations of folAmix the growth rate of evolved strain becomes markedly reduced to nearly half of the wild type value.
source: However, at lower concentrations of folAmix the growth rate of evolved strain becomes markedly reduced to nearly half of the wild type value and appears to plateau in an intermediate range of folAmix concentrations.
evidence: This is based on growth rate measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The growth rate value at the plateau coincides with that measured for cells grown in thymine alone.
source: The growth rate value at this plateau coincides with that measured for cells grown in thymine alone (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), which is indicative that thymine is the growth-limiting component at these concentrations of folAmix and that cells utilize thymine less efficiently in the absence of the other folAmix components.
evidence: This is based on growth measurements comparing folAmix and thymine alone shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: In the absence of a functional DHFR and in the presence of folAmix D27F mutant strains are extremely resistant to trimethoprim.
source: Not surprisingly, in the absence of a functional DHFR and in the presence of folAmix D27F mutant strains are extremely resistant to trimethoprim (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on trimethoprim inhibition measurements shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The evolved D27F strain shows an extremely high resistance to trimethoprim (IC50 = 656 ± 78 µg/mL) at very low concentrations of folAmix.
source: We found that in those conditions IC50 for the wild type is similar to that measured in the absence of supplement, yet the evolved D27F strain still shows an extremely high resistance to trimethoprim (IC50 = 656 ± 78 µg/mL).
evidence: This is based on dose-response measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In a total of 12 trajectories all were found to have mutations in thyA and 11 had deoB mutated.
source: Strikingly, in a total of 12 trajectories all were found to have mutations in thyA and 11 had deoB mutated (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing and Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of functional ThyA and especially DeoB were found to be highly deleterious in evolved D27F strains at low folAmix concentrations.
source: Expression of functional ThyA and especially DeoB were found to be highly deleterious in evolved D27F strains at low folAmix concentrations, as shown Figure 5 D-E, whereas no significant change in growth was observed upon expressing inactive mutants.
evidence: This is based on complementation experiments shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: D27N strain had a point mutation (P74S) in the gene nanM that encodes N-acetylneuraminate mutarotase.
source: Strain D27N had a point mutation (P74S) in the gene nanM that encodes N-acetylneuraminate mutarotase, which supports efficient growth form sialic acid as carbon source (Severi et al., 2008), and a point mutation (L44Q) in the gene thyA (discussed below).
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: D27N strain had a point mutation (L44Q) in the gene thyA.
source: Strain D27N had a point mutation (P74S) in the gene nanM that encodes N-acetylneuraminate mutarotase, which supports efficient growth form sialic acid as carbon source (Severi et al., 2008), and a point mutation (L44Q) in the gene thyA (discussed below).
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: D27G strain had a point mutation (A101V) in the gene ymfD that encodes a putative SAM-dependent methyltransferase.
source: Strain D27G had a point mutation (A101V) in the gene ymfD that encodes a putative SAM-dependent methyltransferase and an early stop codon in the gene upp, that encodes the enzyme uracil phosphoribosyltransferase that participates in pyrimidine salvage pathway.
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: D27G strain had an early stop codon in the gene upp, that encodes the enzyme uracil phosphoribosyltransferase that participates in pyrimidine salvage pathway.
source: Strain D27G had a point mutation (A101V) in the gene ymfD that encodes a putative SAM-dependent methyltransferase and an early stop codon in the gene upp, that encodes the enzyme uracil phosphoribosyltransferase that participates in pyrimidine salvage pathway.
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No other mutation was fixed upon evolution of D27G besides the one nucleotide change at the D27 locus of the folA gene, corresponding to the Gly->Cys substitution.
source: Comparison between evolved and naïve D27G strains reveals that no other mutation was fixed upon evolution besides the one nucleotide change at the D27 locus of the folA gene, corresponding to the Gly->Cys substitution described earlier.
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data comparing naïve and evolved D27G strains.

claim: No difference was found in the growth rate profiles of D27G strains with and without mutations in upp and ymfD.
source: No difference was found in the growth rate profiles of these strains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating no obvious impact of mutations in upp and ymfD in favoring the reversion of DHFR function over thyA inactivation.
evidence: This is based on growth rate measurements shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: DeoB catalyzes the interconversion of 2-Deoxy-D-ribose-1-phosphate and 2-Deoxy-D-ribose-5-phosphate.
source: DeoB catalyzes the interconversion of 2-Deoxy-D-ribose-1-phosphate and 2-Deoxy-D-ribose-5-phosphate, and, while the former is necessary for synthesis of dTMP from thymine by DeoA, the latter can be further degraded in glycolysis, through conversion into acetaldehyde and D-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate by DeoC (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about DeoB function.

claim: Inactivating deoB or deoC is an 'economy' solution preventing key metabolite in thymine uptake to be wasted in energy production.
source: Therefore, inactivating deoB or deoC is an 'economy' solution preventing key metabolite in thymine uptake to be wasted in energy production, allowing cells to efficiently use small amounts of thymine available from media supplement for nucleotide synthesis (Dale and Greenberg, 1972).
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolic pathway analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: While deoB+ cells cannot grow at low concentrations of thymine in the media, replacing this precursor by thymidine or dTMP, which provide a deoxyribose moiety, improves the growth of evolved D27F strains transformed with plasmid expressing active DeoB.
source: In agreement with the key role of deoxyribose in limiting thymine uptake, while deoB+ cells cannot grow at low concentrations of thymine in the media, replacing this precursor by thymidine or dTMP, which provide a deoxyribose moiety, improves the growth of evolved D27F strains transformed with plasmid expressing active DeoB (Figures 6B-C).
evidence: This is based on growth measurements shown in Figures 6B-C.

claim: deoB- cells cannot grow on thymidine as the sole carbon source unless complemented with a plasmid expressing wild type DeoB.
source: Moreover, to confirm that the route for deoxyribose degradation into energy production is blocked in evolved mutants, we measured the growth of naïve and evolved cells in the presence of thymidine as the sole carbon source and verified that deoB- cells cannot grow unless complemented with a plasmid expressing wild type DeoB (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on growth measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PCA analysis revealed that both wild type and evolved D27G occupy the same quadrant in the space of two principal components, whereas D27 mutants that are folAmix dependent cluster more closely in another quadrant.
source: To get a glimpse of global proteomics changes we applied PCA analysis which revealed that both wild type and evolved D27G occupy the same quadrant in the space of two principal components, whereas D27 mutants that are folAmix dependent cluster more closely in another quadrant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on PCA analysis of proteomics data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: A clear anticorrelation was observed between proteomic changes upon evolution and initial changes caused by D27F mutation for all mutants, being the strongest for evolved D27G strain.
source: A clear anticorrelation was observed for all mutants (Figure 7A), being the strongest for evolved D27G strain.
evidence: This is based on comparison of Z-scores shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There was a significant increase in the expression levels of proteins involved in glycolysis, fermentation, sugar alcohol degradation and response to low pH in both evolved D27F and D27N with respect to naïve D27F strains.
source: We found a significant increase in the expression levels of proteins involved in glycolysis, fermentation, sugar alcohol degradation and response to low pH, suggesting a metabolic shift towards mixed acid fermentation as a result of adaptation that blocked using derivative of thymidine for glycolysis to save them for DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is based on proteomics analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The levels of proteins involved in DNA restriction/methylation and D-ribose uptake were significantly decreased with respect to naïve D27F in both evolved D27F and D27N strains.
source: On the other hand, the levels of proteins involved in DNA restriction/methylation and D-ribose uptake were significantly decreased with respect to naïve D27F in both evolved D27F and D27N strains.
evidence: This is based on proteomics analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Significant anticorrelation was found between metabolite changes in evolved D27F with respect to naïve D27F and metabolite changes in naïve D27F with respect to wild type.
source: We computed Z-scores for metabolite changes with respect to naïve D27F (ZD27_evo/D27F_naïve) and we found significant anticorrelation with Z-scores obtained for naïve D27F (ZD27F_naïve/WT) (Figure 7B), indicating that metabolite concentrations in evolved strain generally change to partially recover wild type levels, as observed with proteomics.
evidence: This is based on metabolomics analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The pathways significantly enriched in metabolites with the highest Z-scores in evolved D27F were the same as those that had the most significant changes in naïve D27F, with respect to wild type.
source: We found that the pathways significantly enriched in metabolites with the highest ZD27_evo/D27F_naïve scores (>1.96) in evolved D27F were the same as those that had the most significant changes in naïve D27F, with respect to wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: This is based on metabolomics enrichment analysis comparing naïve and evolved strains.

claim: Supplementation with purines strongly inhibited growth of the naïve D27F strain, whereas pyrimidines addition had, at most, a slight stimulatory effect.
source: Surprisingly, supplementation with purines strongly inhibited growth of the naïve D27F strain, whereas pyrimidines addition had, at most, a slight stimulatory effect (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on growth measurements with metabolite supplementation shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In the case of evolved D27F strain, the effect of supplementation of individual nucleotides on growth was comparably weaker or non-existent.
source: In the case of evolved D27F strain, the effect of supplementation of individual nucleotides on growth was comparably weaker or non-existent, indicating that the inhibitory effects were relaxed upon adaptation.
evidence: This is based on growth measurements with metabolite supplementation shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Evolution of D27F and D27N strains blocked supplementary glycolysis pathway by rerouting Deoxyribose towards DNA synthesis while the ensuing metabolic changes lead to significant increase in abundance of glycolysis proteins.
source: Evolution of D27F and D27N strains blocked supplementary glycolysis pathway by rerouting Deoxyribose towards DNA synthesis while the ensuing metabolic changes lead to significant increase in abundance of glycolysis proteins, presumably to compensate for diminished flux of sugar metabolites along the glycolysis pathway (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on proteomics and metabolomics analysis.

claim: Evolved strains show significant increase in abundance of hypoxanthine giving rise to significant drop in abundance of proteins controlled by purR.
source: Another example of metabolite-induced rewiring is purR operon whereby purR is inhibited by purine hypoxanthine. Evolved strains show significant increase in abundance of hypoxanthine giving rise to significant drop in abundance of proteins controlled by purR (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on metabolomics and proteomics analysis.

claim: Mutations in thyA are known to confer trimethoprim resistance in bacterial clinical isolates of S. aureus and H. influenza.
source: Strikingly, mutations in thyA are also known to confer trimethoprim resistance in bacterial clinical isolates of S. aureus (Chatterjee et al., 2008; Kriegeskorte et al., 2014), and H. influenza (Rodríguez-Arce et al., 2017), which emphasizes the need of laboratory studies of microbial adaptation as useful models to tackle serious global threat.
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: E. coli cells challenged with increasing concentrations of trimethoprim in the presence of thymidine repeatedly evolved high levels of resistance by thyA loss-of-function mutations besides acquisition of commonly observed resistant mutations in DHFR.
source: Likewise, a recent study also reported that E. coli cells challenged with increasing concentrations of trimethoprim in the presence of thymidine repeatedly evolved high levels of resistance by thyA loss-of-function mutations besides acquisition of commonly observed resistant mutations in DHFR (Schober et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The point mutation L44Q in thyA is reported to affect the activity of a nearly identical orthologue enzyme.
source: The point mutation L44Q in thyA, reported to affect the activity of a nearly identical orthologue enzyme (Nur-E-Kamal et al., 1994), could have skewed the solution towards further inactivation of thyA by subsequent point mutations in other loci of that gene that were later observed in different trajectories.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Transversions are generally regarded to be less likely than transitions.
source: In this respect, it is rather surprising that D27C mutation was fixed in three trajectories when transversions are generally regarded to be less likely than transitions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mutation frequencies.

claim: folA+ thyA- strains are thymine-dependent.
source: Thymidylate synthase is the only known enzyme in E. coli able to synthetize dTMP de novo from dUMP, and inactivation of thyA inevitably commits the cell to thymine auxothrophy; reversion of DHFR function on the thyA- background is not expected to change this phenotype, as it is known that folA+ thyA- strains are thymine-dependent (Bertino and Stacey, 1966; Schober et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DeoA is part of the deo operon that is induced by high levels of 2-deoxy-D-ribose-5-phosphate.
source: However, DeoA is part of the deo operon that is induced by high levels of 2-deoxy-D-ribose-5-phosphate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the deo operon regulation.

claim: The gene deoB is part of an operon responsible for deoxyribose degradation, that includes deoA, deoC, and deoD, which is under the control of 2-deoxyribose-5-phosphate-inducible deoR repressor.
source: The gene deoB is part of an operon responsible for deoxyribose degradation, that includes deoA, deoC, and deoD, which is under the control of 2-deoxyribose-5-phosphate-inducible deoR repressor (Hammer-Jespersen and Munch-Ptersen, 1975).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the deo operon supported by a citation.

claim: Recent studies investigated evolution of E. coli upon inactivation of non-essential enzymes of carbon metabolism that lead to re-wiring through less efficient pathways.
source: Recent studies investigated evolution of E. coli upon inactivation of non-essential enzymes of carbon metabolism that lead to re-wiring through less efficient pathways (Krüsemann et al., 2018; Long et al., 2018; McCloskey et al., 2018a; McCloskey et al., 2018b; McCloskey et al., 2018c; McCloskey et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: A comprehensive study involving knock outs of >1000 genes classified as essential in yeast has shown that a small percentage of mutants could recover viability after laboratory evolution.
source: Nevertheless, a comprehensive study involving knock outs of >1000 genes classified as essential in yeast has shown that a small percentage of mutants could recover viability after laboratory evolution (Liu et al., 2015), revealing that essentiality can, in some cases, be overcome through adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Loss of essential biosynthetic genes have been observed to occur naturally, under evolutionary conditions where pathway products are provided externally.
source: Loss of essential biosynthetic genes have also been observed to occur naturally, under evolutionary conditions where pathway products are provided externally (D'Souza and Kost, 2016), highlighting a context-dependent nature of essentiality.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Genes that perform essential functions are believed to face higher selective pressure and thus evolve slower.
source: The genes that perform such functions, often classified as essential, are believed to face higher selective pressure and thus evolve slower (Luo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: DHFR has been repeatedly observed to accumulate mutations leading to extremely high drug resistance levels in various experimental evolution studies.
source: As the cellular target of the antibiotic trimethoprim, DHFR has been repeatedly observed to accumulate mutations leading to extremely high drug resistance levels in various experimental evolution studies (Rodrigues et al., 2016; Tamer et al., 2019; Toprak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental evolution studies.

claim: Past efforts to link fitness effects of chromosomal variation in the folA locus encoding DHFR and their biophysical effects on DHFR protein allowed development of an accurate quantitative biophysical model of DHFR fitness landscape.
source: Past efforts to link fitness effects of chromosomal variation in the folA locus encoding DHFR and their biophysical effects on DHFR protein allowed us to develop an accurate quantitative biophysical model of DHFR fitness landscape (Bershtein et al., 2015a; Bershtein et al., 2013; Bershtein et al., 2012; Bershtein et al., 2015b; Rodrigues et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: When treated with DHFR inhibitor trimethoprim, bacterial cells recurrently acquire resistance by high-fitness mutations near the active site of the target protein that decrease drug binding affinity, even at the expense of catalytic efficiency.
source: For example, when treated with DHFR inhibitor trimethoprim, bacterial cells recurrently acquire resistance by high-fitness mutations near the active site of the target protein that decrease drug binding affinity, even at the expense of catalytic efficiency (Rodrigues et al., 2016; Tamer et al., 2019; Toprak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A mixture (folAmix) of adenine, inosine, thymine, methionine and glycine allows cells to overcome DHFR deficiency.
source: To construct these strains we supplemented the growth medium with a mixture (folAmix) of adenine, inosine, thymine (precursor of dTTP), methionine and glycine which allows cells to overcome DHFR deficiency (Howell et al., 1988; Kwon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Only thymine was essential among individual components of folAmix, although growth with thymine alone is slower compared to growth with all folAmix components.
source: We tested D27 mutants for growth in the presence of individual components of folAmix and their different combinations and found that only thymine was essential, although growth with thymine alone is slower compared to growth with all folAmix components (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on growth measurements with different supplement combinations shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: D27N and D27G mutants show slightly better growth at lower concentrations of folAmix than D27F.
source: Interestingly, D27N and D27G mutants show slightly better growth at lower concentrations of folAmix than D27F.
evidence: This is based on growth measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The catalytic efficiencies of D27G and N, albeit extremely low, are 2 orders of magnitude higher than that of D27F.
source: Given that the catalytic efficiencies of D27G and N, albeit extremely low, are 2 orders of magnitude higher than that of D27F, it is possible that such difference could have a beneficial impact at low folAmix concentrations.
evidence: This is based on comparison of kinetic parameters shown in Table 1.

claim: Adaptation to loss-of-function mutations in DHFR, the cellular target of the antibiotic trimethoprim, can lead to high levels of drug resistance.
source: Finally, we show how adaptation to loss-of-function mutations in DHFR, the cellular target of the antibiotic trimethoprim, can lead to high levels of drug resistance.
evidence: This is based on the trimethoprim resistance measurements shown in the results.
